description: Team Iberico combines creativity, curiosity, and a passion for science and technology. Represented by our legendary crew—a gangster pig, penguin, bat, and turtle—we bring humor, ambition, and unconventional thinking to every challenge. Our mission is to transform bold ideas into innovative solutions, push the boundaries of what's possible, and have fun along the way.
summary: ECHO RETURN is a scientific space adventure for secondary-school learners and curious visitors. Operate spacecraft equipment, diagnose motion, acquire image records and bring evidence home. Inspect what Earth received, mark a question and adapt the last observation. Authentic NASA imagery of Bennu makes coverage, detail and engineering choices consequential: the conclusion depends on evidence that actually arrives.
details:
What changed around Bennu’s Nightingale sampling site? ECHO RETURN makes this question playable inside a fictional astronaut-operated spacecraft. NASA’s historical 2019 and 2021 images provide the source evidence. The challenge-listed Design and Develop a Science Mission resource informs the connection between the question, observation requirements, spacecraft allocation, mission operations and verification.

The player performs the investigation. Aim the camera, set its field and detector readout, and hold it through an exposure. The retained raster records the actual sampled field and motion. Live framing and retained-coverage instruments expose the exercise’s whole-patch and landmark requirements. A wide field can preserve contextual landmarks while sacrificing local detail; a higher readout consumes more memory and return capacity. No photograph is unlocked by selecting a product label.

Two fault causes invite different experiments. Whole-spacecraft drift moves both imagers, while a faulty inspection drive moves that head alone. Compare live feeds, counter body motion, or open the service assembly, isolate power, turn the manual bearing and clamp its actual angle. The recovery changes what can be captured. A healthy-equipment flight is also playable.

The Reply is the central mission adaptation. Return evidence at the first contact and hear fictional flight director Nia Calder and scientist Elias Vale respond to the actual receipts. A context-first return prompts a search for readable detail; a detail-first return prompts a search for locatable context. The astronaut can inspect the complete image during contact, compare dates, mark a location and save an observation. That mark and the previous footprint appear on the next live navigator as manual framing references. They do not steer the camera or change the scientific verdict. The astronaut must operate the instrument and acquire the missing evidence. If complementary evidence is already aboard, prioritize its return. If the received set is adequate, conclude without an unnecessary exposure. Replanning preserves fuel, pointing, spent opportunities, closed contacts, held queue decisions and received data.

The recorder holds real image records. Players drag records into their return order and use spacecraft pointing to acquire Earth. Amber blocks show what fits the current contact; green blocks show actual acknowledgments. The central flight grip turns while deflected and fires an opposite braking pulse on release; the steering and braking pulses both consume the modeled reserve. Arrow switches retain precise single-pulse operation. Partial receipts remain partial: three units of a five-unit image are not a complete scientific frame. The final comparison displays complete returned images. Players drag or blink between dates, pin a feature and save a personal observation before defending a local, global or inconclusive account. A mark is not automatically graded and cannot make insufficient evidence sufficient. The response is bounded by the received set; the game cannot establish asteroid-wide change.

All three flight modes are visible before entering the spacecraft. Explorer adds a fuel-consuming body-settling aid. Mission Specialist uses manual body pointing with automatic antenna trim. Commander adds direct manual antenna alignment. All three have verified complete routes with acquisition failure, physical recovery and successful return. Equivalent-input browser checks also verify that assistance changes actual control behavior while leaving the scientific requirements unchanged. Separate browser missions demonstrate an inconclusive partial return and equal three-unit returns with different scientific sufficiency. These checks establish implemented behavior, not human enjoyment or measured learning gains.

Both historical images were already on Earth; OSIRIS-REx was uncrewed. Astronaut operations, characters, dialogue, faults, budgets and outcomes are fictional. Cropping, sampling, motion accumulation and evidence thresholds are declared educational assumptions, not NASA-calibrated instrument limits. The exterior is procedural illustration. NASA’s documented interpretation supports local sampling disturbance, not a new observation or quantitative displacement measurement.

The browser application uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript modules, Canvas and procedural Web Audio. It runs without an account or external runtime assets. Git checkpoints, model tests and actual browser interactions preserved a working fallback while validating recovery, evidence return and source interpretation. The instructional aim is to make mission-design trade-offs observable through action; learning effectiveness has not been measured.
